data.title: Architourism in France: the retro futurist seaside town near Montpellier that’s out of this world
data.description: Built in the 60s and 70s to curb a holiday exodus to Spain, with apartments inspired by Mayan pyramids and featuring ‘intergalactic curves’, La Grande-Motte is having another moment in the sun with fans of modern architecture My dream holiday is a trip back in time. Not to see the results of seismic Pompeii or 15th-century Machu Picchu – although I love both – but somewhere created specifically between the mid 1950s and 1970s, when cities were getting weird. I love postwar architourism, exploring urban planning at its most frenzied and optimistic. I have relished trips to Niemeyer’s Brasília and Le Corbusier’s Chandigarh in India, where the monumental and visionary modernist architecture and interiors are at odds with the minimal population. So La Grande-Motte, the retro futurist folly of a resort town on the southern coast of France, a 30-minute drive from Montpellier, had long been on my “must visit” list. The tourist board of this Occitanie seaside town likes to flag up some superficial parallels between it and the aforementioned cities, but this isn’t a high-concept capital city or administrative hub. It was built in the late 1960s and early 1970s purely to persuade the French to stop going south to the Costa Brava in Spain. As part of an initiative by the French government, a stretch of windswept mosquito-infested coast between Montpellier and Perpignan, including Gruissan and Port Leucate, was reimagined as an alternative to the Côte d’Azur with several new-build beach towns. La Grande-Motte would be the weirdest project. It was made for fun. It’s also well positioned to visit the nearby salt marshes and 13th-century walled-in town of Aigues-Mortes, for when you want to feel as if you’ve ticked a few more holiday boxes. Continue reading...

data.title: ‘I fight pain and fear with art’: how Yayoi Kusama blazed a trail for neurodivergent artists
data.description: The pioneering Japanese artist talked openly about how her mental health and neurodivergence informed her creativity, paving the way for the likes of Turner prize winner Nnena Kalu Yayoi Kusama – who has died at the age of 97 – was 10 when she first started experiencing vivid hallucinations consisting of visual and aural disturbances, which she described as “flashes of light, auras, or dense fields of dots”. A drawing from 1939, of a woman in a kimono assumed to be her mother, shows her obliterated by those dots; they would become Kusama’s artistic obsession. She hallucinated flowers, too. “I was looking at the red flower patterns of the tablecloth on a table, and when I looked up I saw the same pattern covering the ceiling, the windows and the walls, and finally all over the room, my body and the universe”, she once said, when asked about that recurring motif. “I felt as if I had begun to self-obliterate, to revolve in the infinity of endless time and the absoluteness of space, and be reduced to nothingness.” For Kusama, art making was a means of survival. “I fight pain, anxiety, and fear every day, and the only method I have found that relieved my illness is to keep creating art. I followed the thread of art and somehow discovered a path that would allow me to live”, she said in a 2012 interview . In so doing, she became one of the most acclaimed and admired contemporary artists, staging happenings and influencing the pop art movement as a pioneering figure in the New York avant garde. Her exhibitions and major retrospectives draw huge crowds. In 2022, due to enormous public demand, Tate Modern in London extended her Infinity Mirror Rooms show for a whole extra year (it ended up running until 2024). Continue reading...

data.title: ‘He could arch both eyebrows and curl his lips in every direction all at once’: Tim Curry’s five best screen roles
data.description: The actor fully embraced his physical talents and outsized personality with a line in theatrical baddies teetering deliciously on the edge of serious and silly • Tim Curry, star of The Rocky Horror Picture Show and Stephen King’s It, dies aged 80 • Tim Curry on sexuality, surviving a stroke – and 50 years of stardom • Clowns, corsets and kings: Tim Curry – a life in pictures As Dr Frank-N-Furter, the gender-nonconforming alien mad scientist who presides over Richard O’Brien’s glam rock musical, admits two innocents to his gothic castle and induces them into all sorts of delicious naughtiness, Curry is so thrillingly liberated as to seem a menace. An irresistibly appealing menace. Apparently able to arch both eyebrows and curl his lips in every direction all at once, Curry wraps his mouth around the double-entendres and belts out the lyrics with lip-smacking relish, and fully fleshes out this avatar of sexual confidence. The film earned one of the original cult fandoms, the stage musical endures and many other actors have pulled on Frank’s corset and high heels – but the role indelibly and for ever belongs to Curry. data.title: My home state is set to hand a breakthrough to the German far right. It’s a disaster decades in the making | Marcus Böick
data.description: A sense of abandonment could make Saxony-Anhalt the first state government to be solely led by the AfD. But the party’s hollow promises will only make a dire situation worse It was in the summer of 2004 that I stopped understanding my own people. I was standing on a sweltering market square in Aschersleben, the town where I was born, picturesquely situated on the northern edge of the Harz mountains. A large crowd of angry people had gathered in front of a stage to protest about the welfare reforms (or, as many saw them, welfare cuts) introduced by the Social Democratic-Green coalition government under chancellor Gerhard Schröder. They chanted “We are the people!”, waved handpainted placards and seemed utterly beside themselves. I had gone to secondary school nearby, volunteered at the local hospital and interned at the local newspaper: I knew this place. And yet I found myself bewildered. What, exactly, did these deeply aggrieved people want – standing on a freshly renovated, almost idyllic market square? Weren’t things going reasonably well for them? Where did this burning resentment toward the west come from? Wasn’t the east-west divide supposed to be disappearing by now? Marcus Böick is assistant professor in modern German history at the University of Cambridge Continue reading...

data.title: Ratko Mladić, the ‘Butcher of Bosnia’, dies aged 84
data.description: Bosnian Serb commander responsible for Srebrenica massacre dies in prison while serving life sentence for genocide Ratko Mladić, the infamous Serbian general who was serving a life sentence for genocide committed during the Bosnian war, has died in prison in the Hague, a UN official and his lawyer confirmed. Mladić, 84, had been one of the main architects of the policy of ethnic cleansing during the Bosnian war. He was convicted of genocide for orchestrating the 1995 killing of at least 8,000 Muslims in the UN-designated “safe area” Srebrenica , the worst massacre in Europe since the second world war. data.title: Yayoi Kusama’s psychedelic art was at its best when taken in high doses
data.description: With dots that dizzied the viewer, the giddy sensory overload of seeing the grandest installations of her octopuses and giant pumpkins was hard to resist • Yayoi Kusama, Japanese artist who became a global superstar, dies aged 97 • A life in pictures I once had an argument about Yayoi Kusama with Peter Gabriel. Not in person – I’ve never met the prog rock hero. But after I recorded some critical comments on her work for the BBC, I watched the segment only to see Gabriel passionately defending her. My onscreen cynicism seemed harsh indeed compared with his soulful appreciation of all those dots. My scepticism about Kusama started the first time I saw her work at the Museum of Modern Art in New York. The context is significant because after a big dose of Jackson Pollock’s looping, tangled forests of colour and line (colour as line), Piet Mondrian’s pulsing Broadway Boogie Woogie and other great abstract art, Kusama’s dots appeared to me static, planned, predictable. I wasn’t excited or moved. Continue reading...

data.title: An $18bn settlement is a drop in the ocean for Meta – but the tide will still come for it | Chris Stokel-Walker
data.description: This week’s settlement without liability was pragmatic, but it doesn’t change the inevitability of further lawsuits around the world Not many people would count paying $18bn they didn’t expect to when they woke up that morning as a victory. Yet for Meta, the owners of Facebook and Instagram, the agreement with 52 US attorneys general to settle claims that it designed its products to be addictive to children, and misled people about their safety, could be described as a win of sorts. Meta denies wrongdoing, and the amount it plans to pay will be spread over a decade. Some of it is contingent on other big tech firms not named in its case coughing up too. The cash is chump change for Meta, which made around $60bn in profit last year. More damaging to the tech giant in the long run could be the agreement to unwind some of the mechanics it has spent two decades perfecting to keep us on its platforms. Chris Stokel-Walker is the author of TikTok Boom: The Inside Story of the World’s Favourite App Continue reading...

data.title: The Guardian view on child marriage: girls should not be wives | Editorial
data.description: There’s growing agreement that under-18s need to be protected – but international turmoil is pushing many towards wedlock Every minute, 23 girls around the world wed, according to the Girls Not Brides campaign, a coalition of more than 1,000 organisations across 100 countries. No child should be married. But girls are far more likely to be affected than boys, accounting for nine in 10 of those wed before 18, and their spouses are often much older men. The consequences, beyond the immediate threat of sexual violence, include the shortening of their education, increased risks of poverty and domestic abuse, and poor health, including high rates of maternal mortality. In spring, the Center for Global Development thinktank estimated that child marriage costs $175bn annually in lost productivity and increased health risks. The good news is that the last decade has seen a drop in rates; last year alone, Grenada, Bolivia, Burkina Faso, Kuwait and Portugal introduced bans. But there are disturbing signs of regression elsewhere. In May, the Taliban issued a new judicial code enabling child marriage below the previous minimum age of 16, and preventing wives from ending marriages they entered as children if their husbands object. Previous protections were inadequate and often poorly enforced; now even those have been swept away. data.translatedTitle: The Guardian view on child marriage: girls should not be wives | Editorial
data.translatedDescription: There’s growing agreement that under-18s need to be protected – but international turmoil is pushing many towards wedlock Every minute, 23 girls around the world wed, according to the Girls Not Brides campaign, a coalition of more than 1,000 organisations across 100 countries. No child should be married. But girls are far more likely to be affected than boys, accounting for nine in 10 of those wed before 18, and their spouses are often much older men. The consequences, beyond the immediate threat of sexual violence, include the shortening of their education, increased risks of poverty and domestic abuse, and poor health, including high rates of maternal mortality. In spring, the Center for Global Development thinktank estimated that child marriage costs $175bn annually in lost productivity and increased health risks. The good news is that the last decade has seen a drop in rates; last year alone, Grenada, Bolivia, Burkina Faso, Kuwait and Portugal introduced bans. But there are disturbing signs of regression elsewhere. In May, the Taliban issued a new judicial code enabling child marriage below the previous minimum age of 16, and preventing wives from ending marriages they entered as children if their husbands object. Previous protections were inadequate and often poorly enforced; now even those have been swept away. Activists say forced and early marriages have soared since the Taliban returned to power in 2021, thanks to the ban on secondary education and the state of the economy. data.title: The Guardian view on electoral reform: don’t wait for a crisis to fix a broken system | Editorial
data.description: In an era of multiparty politics, first past the post risks generating perverse outcomes that delegitimise the democratic process If the system that elects MPs to Westminster was obviously the most democratic one available, there would be no need to use alternative modes when electing the UK’s devolved assemblies or England’s regional mayors. The fact that first past the post (FPTP) was not preferred when establishing those institutions reflects an acceptance that there are better ways to turn popular opinion into fair political representation. So why should the Commons stick with an inferior system? This question is raised by an amendment tabled to the representation of the people bill, which returns to parliament next week. The call to establish an independent national commission on electoral reform has been endorsed by 185 MPs. Continue reading...

Comté , a hard cheese made from raw cows’ milk in the Jura mountains, is France’s top-selling traditional cheese, with more than 62,000 tonnes produced last year. The government announced on Wednesday that its producers would be granted a temporary change to strict rules on grazing after farmers said extreme heat had scorched their pastures, putting production at risk. data.title: Japan killed 14,000 bears after a rise in deadly attacks on people – but will it work?
data.description: Bears killed 13 people in Japan last year, as a lack of forest foods increased conflicts. Yet some say the country’s controversial cull could threaten the endangered species Every summer, millions of people escape the heat and humidity of Tokyo by heading to the tranquil resort town of Karuizawa in Japan’s Nagano prefecture – just an hour by bullet train from the capital. Here, at the foot of Mount Asama, visitors stroll bamboo-lined pathways, cycle in verdant highlands, and practise the wellness ritual of shinrin-yoku, bathing among the cool hinoki forests. It would be the ideal nature retreat – if it wasn’t for the bears. From June to August, bears often move close to Karuizawa, feeding on the mulberries, ants, leaves and cherry blossoms that grow near the town. Unlike nuts, these foods are low in calories, spurring the bears to seek out further sustenance. “They’re more likely to get close to residential spaces to see what they can find,” says Amelia Hiorns, a British zoologist who previously worked with Picchio Wildlife Research Centre in the town. “This combines with the busiest season for tourists.” Continue reading...

data.title: How decoding beluga whales’ chitchat may save them – and teach us more about ourselves
data.description: From humpbacks learning the latest songs to sperm whales’ ‘clan codas’, drones and AI learning are helping reveal another dimension to the concept of culture In 2015, the whale researcher Valeria Vergara pitched a small tent at the icy water’s edge on Somerset Island in the remote Canadian high Arctic, shrouded in a freezing fog so thick she struggled to see her own hands. She trailed a cord out to the coast and plopped a hydrophone into the water to record the calls of belugas. As many as 1,000 of the whales, accompanied by their newborn calves, frequented the surrounding bay. Belugas’ ceaseless chatter, made up of dozens of unique sounds, is crucial to keeping these creatures connected in the dim, turbid waters of the Arctic. Continue reading...

data.description: Analysis by Institute for Policy Studies found that between 2019 and 2025, CEO compensation increased 41.4% The average CEO of the US’s 100 largest, lowest-paying corporations earned 614 times more than their average worker last year, according to an analysis by the Institute for Policy Studies (IPS). IPS’s latest executive excess report analyzed compensation at the 100 S&P 500 corporations with the lowest median worker pay. Between 2019 and 2025, CEO compensation increased 41.4%, unadjusted for inflation, twice as much as the median worker pay increased at these firms during the same period, at 20.7%. data.title: Marketing meltdown: why has Andrew Garfield’s new film suddenly added Robin Hood?
data.description: Paul Greengrass drama The Uprising was supposed to be a historical epic about the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 – but a strange new campaign has inserted a surprising figure Nobody likes to have the full plot of a movie spoiled before they’ve even seen it. However, sometimes this can be taken to the extreme. Take the new Paul Greengrass movie, The Uprising, for example. It is two weeks away from release and, not only does nobody know the plot, but nobody seems to know what it is even about. Seriously, nobody at all. The film’s distributors just spent yesterday squabbling in public about whether Robin Hood was in it or not. Here’s what we know so far. Initially, all the trailers and promotional materials made The Uprising look like a film about the Peasants’ Revolt that tore through England in 1381. And this was very exciting, since the revolt was a thrilling moment in history that has been bizarrely underserved by Hollywood over the years. Most excitingly of all, though, it sounded like it fit exactly into Greengrass’s wheelhouse; full of action and realism and political awareness. Continue reading...

data.title: Idiots review – throwback bro comedy is an entertaining summer seat-filler
data.description: Dave Franco and O’Shea Jackson Jr lead a goofy roadtrip comedy that is just sharp enough to keep you strapped in Idiots is billed as a return to the raunchy bro comedies of the 2000s like Pineapple Express and The Hangover and about halfway through there is a visual gag involving bodily functions that is so revolting, so unexpected and so genius that it comes close to them. For a moment, I was transported back to the mix of delight and disgust I felt upon watching a ‘90s Farrelly Brothers movie when I was far too young: How is this allowed? Described as an “earnest-dipshits-on-the-road screwball comedy” by director Macon Blair ( I Don’t Feel at Home in This World Anymore , The Toxic Avenger), this R-rated indie comedy can’t entirely deliver on that enticingly deranged promise, but it has enough testosterone-fueled transgression to make its runtime breeze by. Dave Franco plays Mark, a doofus with a neck tattoo who expresses affection for his fellow man by slapping them on the jowls. When he is invited to vacate his job at a call center – which he has been coasting through by playing gory video games and sneaking shots of whiskey at his desk – he teams up with with Davis (O’Shea Jackson Jr) for a dodgy under-the-table job involving transporting wayward teens to rehab. Their first charge is Sheridan (Mason Thames), a moody influencer who has made a name for himself by playing cruel stunts on members of the public like an off-brand Jake Paul. Like Harold & Kumar before it, the road trip is an obvious but effective ruse for Idiots’s freeform, THC-addled approach to storytelling which finds the trio jumping from country diner to crummy motel to a Slavic granny’s living room as Sheridan attempts to derail his passage to rehab. Continue reading...

data.title: Dalliance review – a rare drama so beautifully written you will be instantly devoted
data.description: Hugo Weaving stars in this wonderful Australian series about old friends in their 60s. It is a feast of hilarity and heartbreak – and there needs to be more TV like it With Dalliance, television continues its brave expeditions into unknown narrative lands. It was first forced to venture into women’s stories (using female writers, directors, stars and, oh my goodness, sometimes it was just wall-to-wall womanity, you know?) in the post-Weinstein years. Previously unassailable figures were toppling like ninepins and investors needed to take refuge in those unlikely to have problematic pasts who were likely to tank projects the moment any reporter turned a beady eye upon them. That turned out quite well. Women were not as boring as we had been led to believe, and were often capable of anchoring quite interesting, intelligent or funny shows. Sometimes they were all three at the same time, even if they weren’t called Fleabag. Continue reading...

data.title: Colony review – zombies return to the mall with a fresh and frenzied range of scares
data.description: This time the ranks of the undead have acquired a hive mind, making them even more formidable adversaries. Can a maverick academic save the day? Here is another frenzied K-zombie action-horror from Yeon Sang-ho, the director of Train to Busan and Peninsula . Colony is frontloaded with 10 minutes of sciencey exposition and setup during which a biotech CEO mentions maze-solving slime mould and the pioneering work of the entomologist William Wheeler on the hive minds of ant colonies. Then the CEO is injected with a disgruntled former employee’s bright green liquid tech – it always needs to be bright green in such circumstances – and becomes the first victim of a bio-terror attack that traps a small cross-section of South Korean society in a tower block with hordes of fast-moving rabid flesh-munchers. An hour and three quarters of goopy, bloody mayhem ensue. An upscale shopping mall occupies the lower floors of the tower, and it takes some nerve to give your zombie film much the same setting as Dawn of the Dead, the masterwork of the godfather of the genre George A Romero . Thankfully Colony can boast an innovation: these zombies have a hive mind, an emergent collective intelligence that makes them more formidable adversaries than your average braindead stumbler. The moment that one of the infected notices you and screams, as in Invasion of the Bodysnatchers, they all turn and attack. Continue reading...

data.title: Song & Dance album review – Jacques Forestier’s impressive debut has persuasive rhythmic poise
data.description: Jacques Forestier/Boris Kusnezow (Warner Classics) The Canadian violinist’s album definitely does what it says on the tin: from Bartók to Ernst, there is a quiet and beguiling eloquence to his playing Perhaps the most promising thing about this impressive debut album from Jacques Forestier , the young Canadian violinist who tied in first place at the 2024 Joseph Joachim Competition, is the way it lives up to its title. There’s a swing to the way he and the pianist Boris Kusnezow play Bartók’s six Romanian Folk Dances that extends even into the quiet movements, which sound distant and beguiling. Wieniawski’s Polonaise de Concert comes across as a dance rather than just a flashy showpiece. Bach’s D minor Sarabande is framed by movements from Ysaÿe’s solo Sonatas. All have persuasive rhythmic poise. Continue reading...

data.title: The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout audiobook review – brilliant portrait of an existential crisis
data.description: A teacher’s private anxieties are subtly combined with political events in this Booker-listed tale set in coastal Massachusetts Artie Dam is a much-loved history teacher from coastal Massachusetts famed for his white socks and old sneakers and who sees a growing hopelessness in his young students. Not only are they dispirited by the state of the world, but they also believe they won’t be able to achieve their professional dreams. Their feelings of dread and ennui are shared by Artie who is aghast at the imminent re-election of a cruel and divisive leader (who remains nameless). Artie is also lonely in the company of his wife, Evie, a therapist who comes from a wealthy family and is dismissive of her “soft” spouse. Artie realises he doesn’t truly know Evie, and she doesn’t care to know him. He traces their loss of connection to their son Rob’s car accident a decade ago in which Rob survived but his girlfriend Heather was killed. Such is Artie’s desolation that he contemplates suicide, if only he can find a way of doing it discreetly. But something happens while he is sailing in his boat that changes his mind. Later, a revelation from his son further shifts his perspective on his relationships. Continue reading...

data.title: Billy Strings: So Much for Goodbyes review – staggering, stirring songs of grief draw the blues out of bluegrass
data.description: (Reprise) The crossover star’s introspective sixth album is full of memories of his mother, who died in 2025, bringing his dextrous guitar to songs rooted in tradition and yearning On the face of it, 2025 was a landmark year for Billy Strings. His fifth album, Highway Prayers , won him his third Grammy. The first bluegrass album in more than 22 years to debut at the top of the US album sales chart, it confirmed him as the genre’s biggest crossover star in decades. He was feted by everyone from Bob Dylan to Post Malone to Willie Nelson, the latter describing him as “the John Coltrane of bluegrass”, a pretty impressive soubriquet in anyone’s book. As the New York Times noted , he was now capable of filling the arena-sized venues that his idols – Doc Watson, Clarence White, Tony Rice, Béla Fleck – could never have dreamed of performing in, packing them out with an audience that look less like traditional bluegrass aficionados than Deadheads: a vast, mobile, hippy-ish army that call themselves Goats. They’re presumably drawn by the ease with which Strings occupies the no man’s land between country and expansive, psychedelically informed improvisation, his willingness to put acoustic guitar through umpteen effects pedals and stretch out songs for 20 minutes on stage. It’s a side of Strings’ music that’s only hinted at on Highway Prayers’ follow-up: as Burn the Other End and Lucid Daydream draw to an end, they briefly unravel into a kind of abstraction that you can imagine as a jumping-off point for heady, out-there exploration live. But So Much for Goodbyes is an album more concerned with introspection, and understandably so. In the midst of 2025’s successes, Strings’ mother died of an overdose. His chaotic upbringing is a matter of record. His father died of a heroin overdose when he was two, both his mother and his stepfather were addicted to meth and he left home at 14 on the grounds that “there was no food in the house and my parents were strung out”. But Strings said he had “no idea” she had relapsed, and her death seeps into every corner of the album: its title and cover art – based on a collage his mother was working on the night she died; the concluding instrumental that bears her name, Debra’s Waltz; the songs that, on the surface, appear to have nothing to do with her passing. Continue reading...

data.title: Kolkhoz by Emmanuel Carrère review – intricate portrait of an elite French family
data.description: The author of The Adversary and Yoga unearths a history that includes the Nazis, Russia, and the Académie Française When Emmanuel Carrère’s mother, Hélène, died in 2023, at the age of 94, President Macron spoke at her memorial. She had been “perpetual secretary” of the Académie Française, in effect its head, and 200 people gathered at Les Invalides in Paris to pay tribute. Emmanuel’s father, Louis, was there too, in a wheelchair, only half aware of what was going on. This 400-page memoir, translated into English by John Lambert, is a homage to both parents and the unlikely history that brought them together. It’s also an act of reparation towards Hélène, whom Emmanuel worshipped as a child but upset as an adult by publishing a book that she’d forbidden him to write. Hélène grew up in stateless poverty in Paris, the daughter of Georges Zourabichvili, whose parents had fled Georgia in 1921, and Nathalie von Pelken, who as a child had six governesses, one for each day excluding Sunday. Though “the magical world of the fallen Russian aristocracy” was the backdrop, conditions were tough, not least after Georges disappeared in 1944, murdered by partisans for alleged Nazi collaboration. Hélène was 15 at the time and unsuccessfully tried to hide the truth about George’s death from her younger brother, Nicolas. Continue reading...

data.title: Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy review – picture-postcard retelling of haunting Minoan myth
data.description: PlayStation 5, Xbox Series S/X, PC; Asobo Studio The medieval franchise is transplanted to Crete, conjuring action-adventure magic from familiar ingredients The path in Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is a familiar one. Amid ancient ruins and sun-dappled gorges, a young woman, Sophia, dutifully treads the same footsteps as a Minoan warrior from millennia ago, one with whom she seems to share a visionary connection. The “resonance” between these two characters is made clear by their echoing actions – a crank pushed in the bronze age that still works in the medieval present, for example. Through these spliced timelines, it becomes clear that Sophia, compelled by her supernatural gift, possesses little agency. Destiny beckons her forwards. This is a smart meta concept for a game that, at its most basic level, boils down to keeping your left thumb planted firmly on the analogue stick, always pushing Sophia onwards in linear fashion. You jostle her through ornate corridors rendered as higgledy-piggledy pirate camps and cobbled Venetian streets. For the greater part of the game, you propel her through the Minoan remains of Crete, which harbour a dark and terrible secret. It is classic third-person action-adventure fare, building on the template laid down by the likes of Tomb Raider and then refined and complicated by titles such as The Last of Us . Little, from an interactive perspective, surprises: you dash, vault and swing between teetering podiums, squeeze through tiny gaps in rock and crouch behind conveniently placed walls to avoid enemies. data.title: Trainwatch – alone with your thoughts on a railway line to nowhere
data.description: The flat routines of a dead end railway job screen out an approaching menace in a quietly intriguing game from the indie developer of  Cat Lady and Lorelai Lonely jobs have provided excellent material for independent video games over the years. From Papers, Please to Firewatch to The Stanley Parable , players have been happy to spend hours dwelling in depressing cubicles or rural hideaways, usually because there is an intriguingly hidden point to it all. In Trainwatch, a character named Troy has taken a seemingly godforsaken job as a railway worker in an unnamed desolate backwater. His main task over the course of a single month is to manage a level crossing, closing the gate whenever a train comes, while also carrying out daily chores such as cooking and washing. It sounds serene, but Troy is also running away from something. The other stipulations are that he stays sober and calls his wife every night. And there is something lurking in the fog at the edges of the fields – one day he must face it. Continue reading...

data.title: Jeers, walkouts, stage invasions: will Catarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists trigger British audiences too?
data.description: It has inspired violent protests from Norway to Rome – and now it’s hitting the UK. Playwright Tiago Rodrigues explains why the far-right speech at the drama’s climax has proved so incendiary In February, turbulent scenes inside a German theatre made headlines around the globe. During the final act of a play at Schauspielhaus theatre in Bochum, the audience first jeered and whistled at a performer in the role of a far-right politician. An orange lobbed from the auditorium narrowly missed its target; eventually, two spectators climbed on to the stage and tried to wrestle the actor off. News of the incident travelled around the world: it seemed a bizarre throwback to a world in which people were not able to tell the difference between art and real life, like 19th-century Parisians stampeding out of a cinema after watching a train hurtle towards the camera. For the man who wrote the play, however, it was nothing unusual. “I was not surprised by the reaction,” says Portuguese playwright Tiago Rodrigues. “I was surprised by the fact that it was so surprising for so many people.” He describes the audience’s reaction to his play Catarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists as “very intense”, but also “typical”. Continue reading...

data.title: ‘The technique was revolutionary’: Ha Chong-Hyun, the 91-year-old South Korean artist who turned painting inside out
data.description: In his trailblazing work, paint is pushed through the back of hemp to create spare, striking paintings. Abstraction is a form of rebellion, he says – and he has no intention of slowing down In the early 1970s, the Korean artist Ha Chong-Hyun had a simple but novel idea: why not apply oil paint to the back of a surface rather than the front? Instead of canvas, he stretched pieces of hemp, a coarse and loosely woven fabric, and pushed the thick oil paint through the holes in the cloth. For each work he used a single colour, in a neutral or muted tone such as white or brown. On the “front” side, he then moved the paint around with various handmade tools to create something akin to brushstrokes. Ha, now 91, has remained dedicated to this technique, known as the “back-pressure method” ( bae-ap-bub in Korean), ever since. He titles every piece Conjunction – because for him the work is essentially about the coming together of artist and material – along with numbers denoting the date of its creation. “The technique he developed was really revolutionary. It hadn’t been done before,” says Max Bossier, director at Lisson Gallery in London, where a selection from this decades-spanning body of work, alongside several of Ha’s earlier artistic experiments, will go on view in September. Continue reading...

data.title: Hot ticket: UK’s first sauna theatre draws swimwear-clad audiences
data.description: The 80-seat venue at Edinburgh fringe combines sauna rituals with theatre, music, storytelling … and sweat Tucked away behind the Summerhall arts centre is the hottest new venue at the Edinburgh fringe … quite literally. The Sauna theatre has proved popular among theatregoers at the world’s largest performing arts festival, with shows inside its purpose-built, 80-seat sauna drawing sweaty, swimwear-clad crowds. Visitors may be forgiven for thinking the sauna is a gimmick, especially at the fringe where absurd, experimental and ludicrous performances are not uncommon. This year they include a man drinking his own urine , someone singing the same song over and over , physical feats of exertion and several fully naked shows. Continue reading...

data.title: How to spot a psychopath: ‘It’s like the difference between a domestic cat and a wild cat’
data.description: People with persistent predatory personalities cause an inordinate amount of pain. Recently, our shared understanding of them has grown – and it could help protect us The classic checklist for psychopathy was developed in 1980 by Prof Robert Hare, who is still the recognised giant of the territory. The 20 traits, which ranged from pathological lying to a lack of empathy, were based entirely on prison populations. This worked because not only did Hare have the benefit of a large sample, with pronounced psychopathic behaviours, but he was able to compare interviews and self-reporting with data collected about the individuals – so inconsistencies could be identified. However, Hare knew this approach was limited. In 1976, he said that he simply didn’t know to what extent his results could be generalised to non-incarcerated psychopaths, including female ones. “Research into the socially successful psychopath is badly needed,” he concluded. Even decades later in the early 2000s, when Hare wanted to look into psychopaths in politics, he still needed to go to prison to find them (Pinochet’s henchmen in Chilean jails). Research into the higher-functioning psychopath – who doesn’t get caught, or maybe doesn’t even resort to crime – has proved elusive, not least because self-reporting questionnaires don’t work. Psychopaths lie; arguably, that’s their main thing. Continue reading...

data.title: Why we’re all hooked on tinned fish
data.description: Sardines, mackerel, herring, pilchards, sprats and anchovies ... canning only makes the umami flavour better. They’re my top choice for pasta Sign up here for our weekly food newsletter, Feast I can’t find it, despite having spent the past 35 minutes looking, but somewhere in the house is The Crisis Cook Book . It’s a standard paperback, postbox-red with white writing on the cover, and full of recipes from chefs including Rowley Leigh , Heston Blumenthal and Jeremy Lee . Not having found it, I needed Amazon to tell me it was published in 2007 and compiled by Nick Lander, at the time the Financial Times’ restaurant correspondent. He asked 28 chefs to donate three recipes – their favourite starter, main course and dessert – and proceeds from the book went to the national homelessness charity Crisis. The reason I needed (and still need – it is now a mission) to find the book is because inside it is Rowley’s recipe for pasta with tinned sardines, fennel, chilli and lemon zest. It’s a recipe that I have made so many times, and for so many years, that I don’t need to look at the book; but, equally, because I’ve made it so many times and so much time has passed, I have no idea how far I have drifted from the original, and want to check. I’ve even written about this recipe in my weekly Guardian column, without referring to the book or even mentioning Rowley! Not that a store-cupboard version of the Sicilian pasta con le sarde (pasta with sardines and wild fennel) is owned by anyone, although Rowley did teach me. Continue reading...

data.title: Honey, I shrunk the wine: why miniature bottles are big again
data.description: Whether they’re consumed as a considered glass for one or something to sip on a short trip, miniature wine bottles are back with a bang In the 1920s, the London wine merchant Berry Bros & Rudd was asked to create a wine cellar for a doll’s house , commissioned by Queen Mary, to showcase the best of British craftsmanship. Designed by Edwin Lutyens, it had running water, electricity, a library of tiny books and, naturally, a wine cellar stocked with 1,200 miniature bottles, including vintage ports, an 1889 Montrachet and top-tier bordeaux. These days, the doll’s house resides in Windsor Castle, but Berry Bros has a replica of that cellar in its own Mayfair cellar, complete with 5ml bottles of those same wines. It is fair to say that this is not representative of the calibre of wine one generally finds in miniature bottles, a format associated with air travel and what I once called “journey juice” – ie, a drop that would last me the six stops from home to London Victoria on a Friday night. Google “miniature bottles of wine” and you’ll overwhelmingly be served examples from the very biggest wine brands in the world. This is also true of canned wines , although I’d argue there’s more interesting wine going into cans than small bottles. Continue reading...

data.title: High in cocoa, high on nostalgia: the chocolate I love most now
data.description: Including, to my surprise, a 100% cacao bar … Although I’m un peu fatiguée of chocolates in bonbon shape with coloured cocoa-butter splashes atop, I appreciate this is the way many chocolates truffles are made. Overcoming that prejudice, I tucked into a box of Scoff chocolates. They were beautifully fresh tasting – they are made in batches throughout the year and the latest batch has just been let loose. I liked every one of the nine flavours I tested, from lemon to malted milk. But the ingredient list is long and a bit mainstream; a cleaner, more artisan approach and this would be a winning brand. Marks & Spencer has brought out some 1980s classics in original packaging for those wanting to go full Rivals: look out for Now! , Jet , Sparks and Coconut Grove and see which chocolate classics they remind you of. My testers loved them. Continue reading...

data.title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for saffron and tomato rice | A kitchen in Rome
data.description: Laborious to harvest and extortionately priced, the sunset-coloured stigmas of the saffron crocus have an extraordinarily warm, pungent taste. Fortunately, however, a little goes a very long way … The saffron crocus has six lilac-purple flowers, three yellow stamens and three orange-red stigmas that extend beyond the petals like the wiry antennae of an insect. The thread-like stigmas have to be picked only by hand when the flowers are fully open, a laborious, finickety job that hasn’t changed much since ancient times. Then, to avoid the colour and flavour fading, the stigmas need to be dried very quickly, a process that reduces their weight by about 80%. Tens of thousands of fiery-looking filaments are required to produce half a kilogram of the dried threads, which make the “hay” or powder we know as saffron and explains the exorbitant cost. Fortunately, just a few threads of this precious spice go a long way. Native to Crete, Iran and south-west Asia, the saffron crocus has been cultivated since the dawn of civilisation for its medicinal properties, as well as for use in cosmetics, perfume, food and as a dye. According to Alan Davidson in The Oxford Companion to Food , the Moguls brought the use of saffron from Persia to India, in particular Kashmir; meanwhile, in the westward direction, the Arabs were cultivating saffron in Spain by AD960, although it was not until the 13th century that cultivation spread to Italy, France, Germany and England, particularly Essex. In his book The Last Food of England , Marwood Yeatman describes the “orderly strips of purple flowers inches apart in beds of up to 10ft wide” growing in a field outside the prosperous, half-timbered Essex wool town of Chipping Walden. “The women (‘crokers’) stooped to lift the crop on damp and dewy September mornings.” By the early 1500s, Chipping Walden had been renamed Saffron Walden. Continue reading...

data.title: Share your tributes and memories of Tim Curry
data.description: We would like to hear your tributes and memories of the performer - whether you met him or admired his work Tim Curry, performer of screen and stage, who made his name as the flamboyant Dr Frank-N-Furter in The Rocky Horror Show, has died aged 80 . Curry got Tony nominations for his varied stage work on Broadway as Mozart in Amadeus, Alan Swann in My Favorite Year and as King Arthur in Monty Python’s Spamalot . He also made a supremely creepy Pennywise the Clown in the 1990 TV adaptation of Stephen King’s It. But above all he is most remembered for one role: Dr Frank-N-Furter in the Rocky Horror Picture Show (1975), the screen version of the 1973 stage show. Continue reading...

data.title: CIA chief reportedly warns Russia against attacking Nato countries on visit to Moscow – US politics live
data.description: Kremlin dismisses US media reports after John Ratcliffe meeting as ‘scare stories’, as Pentagon policy chief prepares to meet Nato secretary general Sign up for the Breaking News US email On Wednesday, Trump officially signed a proclamation on Wednesday that suspends higher tariffs on 300,000 metric tons of foreign beef imports for 90 days. This comes after backlash to the proposal – designed to lower grocery costs for Americans in the run-up to the November midterms. Several Republicans – in states with sizable cattle farming industries – have criticized the policy, saying it is a short term solution that will stymie ranchers’ ability to rebuild their herds. Four leading livestock and agricultural organizations also wrote a letter to the president on Wednesday urging him to reverse course. “Flooding the market with discounted foreign beef is not the way to rebuild the American cattle herd, strengthen food security, or lower grocery bills in a lasting way,” the groups wrote. data.title: Apollo 15’s Genesis Rock, found in 1971, revealed a piece of the Moon’s 4-billion-year-old crust
data.description: Apollo 15 astronauts discovered an unusually bright rock near Spur Crater on the Moon.  This sample, known as the Genesis Rock, is an anorthosite and about four billion years old.  Scientists believe it represents a piece of the Moon's primordial crust.  Its mineral composition offers valuable clues about early lunar geological history.  This ancient sample continues to aid understanding of the Moon's evolution.

data.title: Australian platypuses rescued during drought quickly rebuilt their home ranges after returning to the wild

data.title: Inondations au Népal et au Tibet : « L’origine du drame est un glissement de terrain qui a entraîné avec lui un glacier »
data.description: Si les volumes de roches et de glace qui se sont décrochés dans l’Himalaya n’ont pas encore été quantifiés, le glaciologue Adrien Gilbert estime déjà, dans un entretien au « Monde », que cette catastrophe est d’une ampleur exceptionnelle.
data.translatedTitle: Floods in Nepal and Tibet: “The origin of the tragedy is a landslide which brought with it a glacier”
data.translatedDescription: Although the volumes of rocks and ice that fell away in the Himalayas have not yet been quantified, glaciologist Adrien Gilbert already estimates, in an interview with Le Monde, that this catastrophe is of exceptional magnitude.

data.title: Rima Hassan : des centaines de tweets, des dizaines de plaintes et un procès pour « apologie du terrorisme »
data.description: La députée européenne de La France insoumise doit être jugée en octobre pour un tweet citant l’un des auteurs de l’attentat de l’aéroport de Tel-Aviv en 1972. « Le Monde » retrace deux années et demie de polémiques et de procédures judiciaires associées à la principale figure de la cause palestinienne en France, entre provocations et liberté d’expression.
data.translatedTitle: Rima Hassan: hundreds of tweets, dozens of complaints and a trial for “apology of terrorism”
data.translatedDescription: The European MP for La France insoumise must be judged in October for a tweet quoting one of the perpetrators of the Tel Aviv airport attack in 1972. “Le Monde” retraces two and a half years of controversies and legal proceedings associated with the main figure of the Palestinian cause in France, between provocations and freedom of expression.

data.title: Ratko Mladic, général serbe condamné pour génocide après la guerre de Bosnie-Herzégovine, est mort
data.description: Artisan militaire du projet de « Grande Serbie », ce général a été condamné en 2017 pour « génocide, crimes contre l’humanité et crimes de guerre » durant la guerre de Bosnie-Herzégovine par les juges du Tribunal pénal international pour l’ex-Yougoslavie. Incarcéré à La Haye, il est mort le 27 août, à l’âge de 84 ans.
data.translatedTitle: Ratko Mladic, Serbian general convicted of genocide after the Bosnia-Herzegovina war, is dead
data.translatedDescription: A military architect of the “Greater Serbia” project, this general was convicted in 2017 of “genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes” during the Bosnia-Herzegovina war by the judges of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. Incarcerated in The Hague, he died on August 27, at the age of 84.

data.title: Guerre en Iran : « Le monde semble rappeler chaque jour aux Européens qu’ils n’ont pas la capacité d’influencer les décisions prises aux Etats-Unis »
data.description: En 2015, la diplomatie européenne était au cœur des négociations sur le nucléaire iranien. Six mois après le conflit déclenché par les Etats-Unis et Israël, elle est écartée des discussions. Dans une tribune au « Monde », le politiste Pierre Ramond rappelle le contexte spécifique de l’accord de 2015.
data.translatedTitle: War in Iran: “The world seems to remind Europeans every day that they do not have the capacity to influence decisions made in the United States”
data.translatedDescription: In 2015, European diplomacy was at the heart of the Iranian nuclear negotiations. Six months after the conflict triggered by the United States and Israel, she was excluded from discussions. In a column in “Le Monde”, political scientist Pierre Ramond recalls the specific context of the 2015 agreement.

data.title: A Rome, le centre social Spin Time, symbole des luttes de gauche, dans le viseur du gouvernement Meloni
data.description: Centre autogéré au cœur de la capitale italienne, Spin Time a été évacué après un incendie, fin juillet. L’avenir du lieu, où logeaient 400 personnes, est compromis, alors que la présidente du conseil a fait de la fermeture de ces établissements l’un de ses chevaux de bataille.
data.translatedTitle: In Rome, the Spin Time social center, symbol of left-wing struggles, in the sights of the Meloni government
data.translatedDescription: A self-managed center in the heart of the Italian capital, Spin Time was evacuated after a fire at the end of July. The future of the place, where 400 people were staying, is compromised, while the president of the council has made the closure of these establishments one of her main priorities.

data.title: Violences dans le périscolaire à Paris : Anne Hidalgo et Patrick Bloche directement visés par des plaintes
data.description: L’avocate des familles assure que les plaintes s’appuient sur « des éléments probants », montrant que l’ex-maire et son ancien premier adjoint avaient « connaissance d’un péril grave et imminent auquel étaient exposés les enfants », « placés sous leur responsabilité », mais qu’il y a eu un « déni complet ».
data.translatedTitle: Violence in extracurriculars in Paris: Anne Hidalgo and Patrick Bloche directly targeted by complaints
data.translatedDescription: The families' lawyer assures that the complaints are based on "convincing evidence", showing that the ex-mayor and his former first deputy had "knowledge of a serious and imminent danger to which the children were exposed", "placed under their responsibility", but that there was a "complete denial".

data.title: Le procès du « cerveau » présumé du 11-Septembre, Khalid Cheikh Mohammed, commencera le 5 juin 2028
data.description: Khalid Cheikh Mohammed a été capturé au Pakistan en 2003 avant son transfert à la prison de Guantanamo. Il est entre-temps passé par les prisons secrètes de la CIA en Pologne pour y subir des séances d’interrogatoire sous la torture.
data.translatedTitle: Trial of alleged 9/11 'mastermind' Khalid Sheikh Mohammed to begin June 5, 2028
data.translatedDescription: Khalid Sheikh Mohammed was captured in Pakistan in 2003 before his transfer to Guantanamo prison. In the meantime, he passed through the CIA's secret prisons in Poland to undergo interrogation sessions under torture.

data.title: « Face à Ebola, il faut multiplier les capacités actuelles de la riposte » : l’appel du directeur de l’OMS dans la lutte contre le virus Bundibugyo en RDC
data.description: Trois cadres d’organisations internationales de santé publique, dont le directeur de l’Organisation mondiale de la santé, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, détaillent, dans une tribune au « Monde », les pistes à suivre pour enrayer l’épidémie qui se propage à grande vitesse en République démocratique du Congo.
data.translatedTitle: “Faced with Ebola, we must multiply the current response capacities”: the appeal of the WHO director in the fight against the Bundibugyo virus in the DRC
data.translatedDescription: Three executives from international public health organizations, including the director of the World Health Organization, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, detail, in a column in “Le Monde”, the avenues to follow to stop the epidemic which is spreading at high speed in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

data.title: Caen : une voiture fonce sur des piétons, deux morts et neuf blessés

data.title: Robots humanoïdes : en Chine, le spectacle des Jeux mondiaux et l’épreuve du réel
data.description: Plus grands, plus agiles, plus nombreux : les robots humanoïdes chinois ont fait forte impression lors des compétitions organisées à Pékin. Mais, derrière le divertissement, une industrie encore balbutiante cherche toujours la clé pour les rendre autonomes et donc utiles.
data.translatedTitle: Humanoid robots: in China, the spectacle of the World Games and the test of reality
data.translatedDescription: Bigger, more agile, more numerous: Chinese humanoid robots made a strong impression during competitions held in Beijing. But, behind entertainment, an industry that is still in its infancy is still looking for the key to making them autonomous and therefore useful.

data.title: En Indonésie, les îles de Bornéo et de Sumatra en proie à des feux de tourbière gigantesques et incontrôlables
data.description: Alors que le phénomène El Niño accroît l’intensité de la saison sèche, des exploitants de plantations d’huile de palme ou de bois à papier sont soupçonnés de défricher des concessions forestières par le feu. Le président indonésien, Prabowo Subianto, a fait part de sa détermination à les punir.
data.translatedTitle: In Indonesia, the islands of Borneo and Sumatra plagued by gigantic and uncontrollable peat fires
data.translatedDescription: While the El Niño phenomenon increases the intensity of the dry season, operators of palm oil or paperwood plantations are suspected of clearing forest concessions by fire. Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has expressed his determination to punish them.

data.title: Comunidade montanhista chora pelo Nepal e vídeo mostra destruição
data.description: No momento em que começo a escrever esta coluna, que obviamente ia falar de assunto mais leve, o mundo do montanhismo está paralisado, tentando entender o que aconteceu na meca das escaladas, as montanhas da cordilheira do Himalaia, no Nepal, atingida na manhã desta quarta-feira (26) por uma tragédia impressionante cujas vítimas o noticiário local avalia em milhares, embora o governo inicialmente tenha admitido 160 mortos e 484 desaparecidos . As primeiras informações citam a probabilidade de o terremoto de 4.4 registrado na região ter descolado um grande bloco de gelo de algum glaciar, provocando uma avalanche que teria chegado até os rios Bhote Coshi e Trisuli, na região central do país asiático, na fronteira com o Tibete, gerando a massiva inundação que levou tudo pela frente por quilômetros e cujas imagens correram o mundo. Leia mais (08/26/2026 - 23h00)
data.translatedTitle: Mountaineering community mourns Nepal and video shows destruction
data.translatedDescription: At the moment I start writing this column, which was obviously going to talk about a lighter subject, the world of mountaineering is paralyzed, trying to understand what happened in the mecca of climbing, the mountains of the Himalayan range, in Nepal, hit this Wednesday morning (26) by an impressive tragedy whose victims the local news estimates in the thousands, although the government initially admitted 160 dead and 484 missing. The first information cites the probability that the 4.4 earthquake recorded in the region had detached a large block of ice from a glacier, causing an avalanche that would have reached the Bhote Coshi and Trisuli rivers, in the central region of the Asian country, on the border with Tibet, generating the massive flood that took everything in front of it for kilometers and whose images spread around the world. Read more (08/26/2026 - 11:00 pm)

data.title: Nepal flash flood: What triggered the deadly Himalayan disaster?
data.description:
A devastating flash flood has struck Nepal’s Rasuwa district near the Tibet border, leaving at least eight people dead and hundreds reported missing. The disaster swept through the Bhote Koshi River basin, causing widespread destruction to villages, roads, bridges and major hydropower projects.

Authorities say hundreds of travellers are unaccounted for, including foreign tourists from several countries. Rescue teams, supported by helicopters and emergency personnel, are continuing search and evacuation operations across the affected region.

Authorities say hundreds of travellers are unaccounted for, including foreign tourists from several countries. Rescue teams, supported by helicopters and emergency personnel, are continuing search and evacuation operations across the affected region.
